questions.question: What is a dataclass in Python, and how do type hints make it better?
questions.title: Typed Dataclasses in Python
questions.direct_answer: A dataclass is a normal Python class decorated with `@dataclass`; the decorator uses annotated fields to generate methods such as `__init__`, `__repr__`, and `__eq__`. The hints document each field and let static checkers verify construction and use, but they do not validate field values at runtime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand generated data-model methods, annotated fields, defaults, and the lack of automatic runtime type validation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing a dataclass as a validation library or assuming a frozen dataclass makes every nested value immutable.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that field order drives the generated constructor and that `default_factory` creates a fresh mutable value per instance.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `@dataclass` generates common methods from class fields.
Annotated fields become parameters in the generated `__init__` by default.
Type hints help checkers and editors but do not validate constructor values at runtime.
Use `field(default_factory=...)` for a fresh mutable default per object.
Options such as `frozen`, `order`, `slots`, and `kw_only` change generated behaviour.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A dataclass is still a normal Python class. Adding `@dataclass` asks Python to build routine methods from the fields declared in the class. With `name: str` and `price: float`, it normally creates an `__init__` that accepts those values, a useful `__repr__`, and value-based `__eq__`. The class can still contain ordinary methods and properties.

Annotations such as `name: str` tell the decorator which names are instance fields. They also tell editors and static type checkers what values are expected. A checker can flag `Product(name=42, price="free")`, and an IDE can offer completion for the attributes. This makes the model easier to understand and check before it runs.

Field order becomes constructor order, and required fields must come before fields with defaults. A collection should use `field(default_factory=list)` so every object receives its own list. Options such as `slots=True`, `kw_only=True`, `order=True`, and `frozen=True` change the generated behaviour. `frozen` prevents normal field reassignment, but it does not make a nested list immutable.

`Product("Keyboard", 75.0)` uses the generated constructor, while `discounted()` is a normal method written by the developer. The example also gives each product a fresh `tags` list. The hints document the intended values, but data from JSON, a form, or another external source still needs separate parsing or runtime validation.

A dataclass fits an object with a fixed set of fields, useful value equality, and light behaviour. A hand-written class is clearer when construction has several steps, invariants must always be enforced, or the public API should hide the stored state. `__post_init__` can calculate derived fields or perform simple checks, but it does not turn annotations into automatic type validation.

sections.title: From field declarations to an ordinary class
sections.content:
When the class body finishes, the decorator examines its fields and configuration, then adds methods to the class. An annotated field without a class-level value is required by the generated initializer. A field with a default becomes optional, and field order becomes constructor parameter order unless keyword-only behaviour is selected.

The generated equality method compares instances as ordered tuples of their fields and generally requires the same class. `repr` displays field names and values, which is useful during debugging. `frozen=True` prevents normal rebinding of fields, but a nested list or other mutable object can still change; frozen is not deep immutability.

A dataclass can contain normal methods, computed properties, class variables, and `__post_init__`. The latter is useful for derived fields or simple invariant checks after generated assignment, though applications that parse untrusted input often use a dedicated validation layer.

sections.title: What the decorator creates
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  F[Annotated class fields] --> D[@dataclass decorator]
  O[Decorator options] --> D
  D --> I[Generated __init__]
  D --> R[Generated __repr__]
  D --> E[Generated __eq__]
  I --> A[Ordinary runtime assignments]
  T[Static checker] -->|reads field hints| C[Checks construction and attribute use]
  A -. no automatic type validation .-> C
```

sections.title: A small typed data model
sections.content:
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(slots=True)
class Product:
    name: str
    price: float
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    def discounted(self, percent: float) -> float:
        return self.price * (1 - percent / 100)

keyboard = Product("Keyboard", 75.0)
keyboard.tags.append("hardware")
print(keyboard)
print(keyboard.discounted(20))
```

The decorator creates the constructor, representation, and equality method; the declared method remains normal class behaviour.

questions.question: When should you choose a dataclass instead of a regular class or dictionary?
questions.title: Dataclass vs Regular Class vs Dictionary
questions.direct_answer: Choose a dataclass for a well-defined data record that benefits from generated construction, representation, equality, and static field types. Choose a regular class when creation and invariants need custom control, and use a dictionary for genuinely dynamic key-value data rather than a fixed domain model.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can select a representation from the shape and behaviour of the data.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a dataclass only to save typing even when construction rules or dynamic keys make another model clearer.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate a typed dictionary shape from a runtime dataclass object and mention validation as an independent concern.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use a dataclass for a fixed set of named fields and data-focused behaviour.
Use a regular class when construction, encapsulation, or invariants need full control.
Use a dictionary when keys are dynamic or the value is naturally a mapping.
A dataclass is a runtime object; `TypedDict` values remain ordinary dictionaries.
None of these choices validates untrusted data merely because hints are present.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Choose a dataclass when a value is mainly a record with a stable set of named fields. It provides a generated constructor, readable representation, and value-based equality while remaining a real class. That is a natural fit for an `InvoiceLine` with `description`, `quantity`, and `unit_price`.

A dataclass is not limited to passive fields. `line.total()` can keep a calculation beside the data it uses, and `frozen=True` can prevent normal field reassignment when the record should not change. The generated methods remove routine code; they do not stop the class from having its own methods and properties.

Choose a regular class when object creation has several steps, inputs must be transformed before storage, or every state change must protect an invariant. For example, a bank account may expose `deposit()` and `withdraw()` instead of allowing callers to assign `balance` directly. A custom constructor, factory methods, and private state make that boundary clearer.

Choose a normal dictionary when keys are discovered at runtime or mapping operations are the point of the value. `TypedDict` can describe a fixed dictionary shape to a static checker, but the runtime value is still a plain `dict`; it does not gain generated constructors, equality rules, or instance methods from that annotation.

A dataclass, regular type hints, and `TypedDict` do not automatically prove that decoded JSON contains safe values. Parse and validate untrusted input first, then create the representation that best matches how the program will use it. The choice is about data shape, ownership, and behaviour rather than which syntax is shortest.

sections.title: Dataclasses, mappings, tuples, and data identity
sections.content:
A domain record usually has a stable name and a stable set of attributes. A dataclass makes that identity visible in code and creates instances with attribute access. Its generated equality is also useful when two records with the same field values should compare equal.

A regular class earns its extra code when the public interface should be smaller than the stored state. Factory methods, private attributes, validation during mutation, caching, and multiple internal representations can all make explicit methods clearer than generated field assignment.

A mapping is different: callers work through keys, iteration, membership, and serialization-friendly operations. `TypedDict` adds a static schema to that mapping style; it does not create a normal class instance and cannot provide instance methods. The best representation follows how the program uses the value, not merely which syntax is shortest.

sections.title: Match the representation to the job
sections.content:
| Choice | Best fit | Runtime form | Main trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dataclass | Stable record with named fields and light behaviour | Class instance | Generated public field-oriented API |
| Regular class | Behaviour, encapsulation, controlled construction | Class instance | More code, maximum control |
| `TypedDict` | Fixed dictionary schema for static checking | Plain `dict` | No instance methods or runtime validation |
| Plain `dict` | Dynamic keys and mapping operations | Plain `dict` | Weak static knowledge unless parameterized |

sections.title: A record with behaviour belongs naturally in a dataclass
sections.content:
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class InvoiceLine:
    description: str
    quantity: int
    unit_price: float

    def total(self) -> float:
        return self.quantity * self.unit_price

line = InvoiceLine("Notebook", 3, 4.5)
print(line.description, line.total())
```

The shape is fixed and the calculation belongs to the record. A free-form metadata bag would still be better represented as a dictionary.

questions.question: Why should a dataclass collection field use default_factory?
questions.title: Mutable Defaults in Python Dataclasses
questions.direct_answer: Use `field(default_factory=list)` or another zero-argument factory so each dataclass instance receives a new mutable object. A shared class-level mutable default would let one instance change another instance's data, so dataclasses reject many such defaults instead of silently sharing them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand when defaults are created and why mutable values must be instance-specific.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing `tags: list[str] = []` or calling the factory immediately as `default_factory=list()`.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State that the factory is a zero-argument callable and is invoked for each instance that omits the field.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A mutable default must not be shared by all instances.
Write `field(default_factory=list)`, passing the function rather than calling it.
The factory runs separately for each instance that needs a default.
Use a lambda when construction needs a non-empty fresh value.
Required fields must appear before fields with defaults.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A list written directly in a class body is created when the class is defined, not each time an object is constructed. Reusing that object would make several instances point to the same list. Dataclasses reject many mutable or unhashable direct defaults because this accidental shared state is almost never the intended meaning of a field.

Write `tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)`. The value of `default_factory` is the zero-argument function `list`, not the result of calling `list()`. The generated initializer calls that function only when the caller leaves out `tags`; an explicitly supplied list is used as given.

With a factory, appending `"urgent"` to `first.tags` does not change `second.tags`. The two fields contain equal empty lists at first, but they are different objects. That identity check is the clearest small test of whether the default is safely owned by each instance.

Use a lambda such as `lambda: ["new"]` when each instance needs a fresh non-empty value. Immutable values such as numbers and strings can usually be direct defaults. A factory still makes the field optional in the generated constructor, so required fields must appear before it unless keyword-only field rules are used.

support.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Task:

beats.recallRule: Pass a factory whenever each dataclass instance must receive its own newly created default value.

sections.title: Creation time determines ownership
sections.content:
Class bodies execute once, so an object created there belongs to the class definition unless another mechanism creates per-instance values. A generated initializer using one prebuilt list would reproduce the classic mutable-default problem: many owners would hold the same object reference.

A default factory delays construction until an instance is initialized. The decorator records the callable, and the generated `__init__` invokes it only when no explicit field value was supplied. That makes ownership clear: the new list belongs to that instance.

Immutable values such as numbers, strings, and frozen tuples can usually be direct defaults because they cannot be changed in place. For a custom object, ask about ownership and mutation rather than relying only on its type name. Python 3.11 broadened the dataclass rejection check from a few known mutable built-ins to unhashable defaults as an approximation, but a factory remains the explicit model for fresh state.

sections.title: A factory creates one list per object
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  F[field default_factory=list] --> I1[Create first Task]
  F --> I2[Create second Task]
  I1 --> L1[new list A]
  I2 --> L2[new list B]
  M[Append urgent to list A] --> L1
  L2 --> E[Still empty]
```

sections.title: Prove that the defaults are independent
sections.content:
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Task:
    title: str
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

first = Task("Deploy")
second = Task("Document")
first.tags.append("urgent")

print(first.tags)
print(second.tags)
print(first.tags is second.tags)
```

The program prints `['urgent']`, `[]`, and `False`, showing that the factory produced independent lists.
